issues.legal_issue: A court may enter judgment on admissions drawn from pleadings and other material in the same suit when the admissions leave no genuine controversy over the facts establishing entitlement to relief.
material_facts: The lessor sought possession after terminating a lease for non-payment of rent.
The lessee admitted in its written statement that it had withheld rent and acknowledged the termination notice.
In a separate application in the lessor’s suit seeking relief against forfeiture, the lessee stated that it had no objection to paying rent under the lease and undertook to pay future rent.
The lessee did not specifically deny several material assertions in the lessor’s application for judgment on admissions.
issues.conclusion: The admissions in the pleadings and in the lessee’s application in the same suit could be considered under Order 12 Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the possession judgment could stand.
issues.legal_principle: Order 12 Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure is broader than Order 12 Rule 1: admissions may be in pleadings or otherwise, orally or in writing, and may be inferred from the facts and circumstances. It is an enabling and discretionary provision intended to allow speedy judgment where there is no real controversy. The Court relied on Thorp v. Holdsworth, Charanjit Lal Mehra v. Kamal Saroj Mahajan, Uttam Singh Duggal & Co. Ltd. v. United Bank of India, and Shikharchand v. Mst. Bari Bai. The Court rejected the contention that the first proviso to Order 8 Rule 5 necessarily required independent proof in these circumstances.

rule.if: civil_suit_for_possession and clear_admission_of_landlord_tenant_relationship and clear_admission_of_rent_nonpayment and admission_of_termination_notice

predicates.civil_suit_for_possession: A claimant brought a civil suit seeking possession of property from an occupant.
predicates.clear_admission_of_landlord_tenant_relat: The occupant clearly admitted that the claimant had let the property to the occupant.
predicates.clear_admission_of_rent_nonpayment: The occupant clearly admitted that it had not paid rent due under the lease.
predicates.admission_of_termination_notice: The occupant admitted receiving notice terminating the lease.

issues.definition: When a possession suit includes clear admissions about the landlord-tenant relationship, unpaid rent, and receipt of termination notice, a possession judgment may be entered on those admissions.

issues.legal_issue: A party may not rely on a transaction to obtain a benefit while denying that same transaction to obtain a different advantage.
material_facts: The lessee questioned the lessor’s title and denied that the lessor was entitled to rent under the lease.
In seeking relief against forfeiture, the lessee relied on the lease and stated that it would pay rent under it.
issues.conclusion: The lessee could not adopt those inconsistent positions; the doctrine of election applied.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of election, also described as approbating and reprobating, prevents a party from accepting a benefit under an instrument while rejecting its inconsistent provisions or consequences. The Court relied on Verschures Creameries Ltd. v. Hull and Netherlands Steamship Co. Ltd., as approved in Bhau Ram v. Baij Nath Singh, and on Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao and C. Beepathuma v. Velasari Shankaranarayana Kadambolithaya.

predicates.claims_concern_same_transaction: The party’s claims or applications concern the same transaction.
predicates.party_relies_on_transaction_for_benefit: The party relied on the transaction to seek a benefit or remedy.
predicates.party_denies_transaction_for_other_advan: The party denied the transaction or its effect in order to seek a different advantage.

issues.definition: A party that relies on a transaction for a benefit but denies it for another advantage cannot maintain both positions.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who was inducted by a landlord is generally estopped from denying that landlord’s title in the absence of a claim by a superior title-holder that has displaced the landlord.
material_facts: The lessee admitted that the trust had inducted it as tenant under registered leases.
The lessee challenged the trust’s title, but no superior landlord had evicted or threatened to evict it.
The lessee’s separate suit challenging the trust’s title had been dismissed, and no restoration of that suit was shown.
issues.conclusion: The tenant-estoppel principle applied prima facie, and the lessee was prima facie barred from challenging the lessor’s title in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act estops a tenant, during the continuance of the tenancy, from denying that the landlord had title to the premises at the commencement of the tenancy. The Court distinguished D. Satyanarayana v. P. Jagadish, where a sub-tenant faced eviction by a superior landlord and attorned to that title; no comparable superior-title circumstance existed here.

predicates.tenant_relationship_admitted: The occupant admitted that it entered possession as a tenant under the claimant.
predicates.landlord_inducted_tenant: The claimant inducted the occupant into possession as tenant.
predicates.no_superior_title_displaced_landlord: No superior title-holder evicted the occupant or displaced the claimant as landlord.

issues.definition: When a tenant admits being inducted by a landlord and no superior title has displaced that landlord, the tenant is estopped from denying the landlord’s title.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee who seeks equitable relief against forfeiture while taking inconsistent positions about the lease and lessor may be denied that relief.
material_facts: The lessee sought relief against forfeiture under its lease and stated that it had no objection to paying rent under that lease.
The lessee also denied that the trust was its lessor and challenged the trust’s entitlement to receive rent.
The lessee had failed to pay rent and had adopted inconsistent positions in the related proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The denial of relief against forfeiture was upheld, and the lessee’s inconsistent positions and conduct supported denying equitable relief.
issues.legal_principle: Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act provides an equitable remedy against forfeiture for non-payment of rent. A party seeking that remedy on the basis of a lease cannot at the same time reject the lease or the lessor’s rights under it; the doctrine of election and the party’s conduct are relevant to the equitable determination. The Court relied on the principles in Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao and C. Beepathuma v. Velasari Shankaranarayana Kadambolithaya concerning approbating and reprobating.

rule.if: lessee_seeks_relief_against_forfeiture and rent_unpaid and lessee_relies_on_lease_for_relief and lessee_denies_lease_or_lessors_rights

predicates.lessee_seeks_relief_against_forfeiture: A lessee applied for equitable relief from forfeiture of the lease.
predicates.rent_unpaid: The lessee had failed to pay rent due under the lease.
predicates.lessee_relies_on_lease_for_relief: The lessee relied on the lease as the basis for seeking relief.
predicates.lessee_denies_lease_or_lessors_rights: The lessee also denied the lease or the lessor’s rights under it.

issues.definition: A lessee who seeks relief against forfeiture by relying on a lease while denying that lease or the lessor’s rights may be denied that relief.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may refuse discretionary special-leave interference when the litigant’s conduct in the proceedings makes the requested intervention inequitable.
material_facts: The appeals challenged a High Court judgment affirming a possession decree.
The lessee repeatedly sought adjournments, failed to pursue proceedings diligently, and prolonged the litigation.
After the High Court judgment, the lessee and its members initiated further proceedings that delayed execution of the decree.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere under Article 136 and dismissed both appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 confers plenary, residuary, and discretionary jurisdiction, to be exercised sparingly and in suitable cases; a party’s conduct is relevant to whether that discretion should be exercised. The Court relied on Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala, Preetam Singh v. The State, Municipal Board, Pratabgarh v. Mahendra Singh Chawla, Transmission Corpn. of A.P. Ltd. v. Lanco Kondapalli Power (P) Ltd., Jagraj Singh v. Birpal Kaur, Tanna & Modi v. CIT, Mumbai XXV, and Prestige Lights Ltd. v. State Bank of India.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party sought discretionary appellate intervention in a special-leave appeal.
predicates.repeated_delay_or_negligence: The party repeatedly delayed the proceedings or failed to pursue them diligently.
predicates.conduct_makes_intervention_inequitable: The party’s conduct in the litigation made granting discretionary intervention inequitable.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, repeated delay or negligence that makes intervention inequitable may lead the Court to deny discretionary appellate interference.
